playbook:
When I choose strike, I go to the maximum allowed. Every point of strike above the opponent's guard scores directly, and opponents in this game tend to settle into a fixed mid-level guard (like 4), so max strike earns steady points every round. Half-measures like 5, 6, or 7 strike just mirror the opponent and produce ties — that did not work.

When I choose guard, I also go to the maximum allowed. There is no stated budget linking strike and guard — each is capped independently at the garrison limit — so a high guard costs nothing and scores surplus points whenever it exceeds the enemy strike, while also blocking damage.

When the opponent posts an inspection threat, I ignore it as a reason to play conservatively. The findings docked me even when my filings were plainly within the stated limits, so I cannot avoid the dock by "playing it straight." I treat inspections as a fixed tax the opponent will levy when they can, not as something my choices control.

When a dock is announced, I recompute my effective score (displayed points minus pending docks) before deciding anything, and I do not panic-change my allocation. Max strike and max guard remain the best response; the dock is the same whether I bid high or low, so I keep earning the most per round to outpace it.

When the opponent's history shows a repeated pattern (e.g., the same strike/guard split every round), I exploit it: set strike above their guard and guard above their strike. I do not vary my numbers just to be unpredictable — consistency at the maximum is what won.

When the final round arrives, I commit fully on both stages regardless of the score, since there is no future round to save for.

When I am unsure, I default to 10 strike and 10 guard rather than a "balanced" split; the balanced splits were my losing and tying lines.
